originalEnglish:
sequencing
Every shot in a film is sandwiched within the context of the shot immediately before it and
the shot immediately after it.





Movies are simply a long sequence of individual images. Because the audience can’t walk around the
space or ask the characters questions, your role as the director is to guide them to what they need to
see to understand the story.

The images before and after each image create thematic, informational and geographic context.
Bringing intentionality to how one image relates to the next is the power you have to create a movie
that is cohesive and affecting.

coverage
Many directors shoot solely “coverage.” Coverage is a classic selection of angles within a
scene (maybe a wide shot, a two shot and each actor’s close ups.) that provide the editor with
options in post-production. This mitigates the risk of not having the images you need when
you get to the edit, but leads to generalized, uninspired compositions.

 wideshot                    two-shot                    close-up





The better understanding you have of how the principles of composition and editing work together,
you’ll have more opportunities to think outside the box and create shots that are unique and
affecting– with the confidence to know they’ll cut together!

        reframing coverage
           Instead of starting a shotlist by selecting shots that “cover” you in the
             edit, try writing a shot list that provides “emotional coverage”.

         Ask yourself: have the compositions of the shots in your shotlist covered
          each emotional beat in your scene? Remember that an image is worth
         1000 words, and that the audience should be able to understand what’s
          happening in a scene with no dialogue at all.

context
When watching a movie, the viewer’s brain is trying to deduce 3 things to make sense of each image:
       1. “where am I?”
     2. “what do I know?”
     3. “how do I feel about it?”

When devising your compositions, start by ensuring these questions are answered.
“where am I?”
Have you ever seen a picture of a house or apartment in a real estate listing, then when
you go take a tour it somehow looks totally different than you pictured? That’s what’s
happening in your movie! It’s the director’s responsibility to keep the viewer oriented in a
2D representation of a 3D world. We need to give the viewer enough information – and at
the right time – to get oriented within the space. We do this with everything from angles, to
visual landmarks, to eyelines.
geography and orientation
You can establish physical geography by using establishing shots, landmarks, and the 180 line.
establishing shots
Filming multiple angles of your environment before diving into the narrative of a scene will help
orient your audience to their surroundings.




landmarks
In addition to shooting establishing shots, you can include visually memorable indicators of location
in the backgrounds of your scenes.

the axis of action and the 180 rule
The 180 Rule refers to the arc of space the camera is placed in to preserve the viewer’s
geographic understanding of the world.

The 180 Arc is established from The Axis of Action.

The Axis of Action is the midpoint on the direct Line of Action between two
subjects.

Once The Line of Action has been established, every shot must be framed from within
The 180 Arc to preserve the viewer’s spatial orientation.





               A                  B
                                   the line of action
                     character a                “the pov line”        character b
changing or establishing a new axis of action
A new Line of Action can be established in the following ways:
1. A character moves across the line within a single shot.
2. The camera moves across the line within a single shot.
3. A new character enters the scene and establishes a new line of action with an existing character.

        reframing shot lists
            Fix it in preproduction! Consider incorporating eyeline
            delineations within your shotlist. Understanding an eyeline
           plan is crucial to ensuring your images will cut together.

“what do I know?”
Every shot in a film will either ask a question or provide an answer.

When deciding on the composition of a shot, understand if it is asking a question
(interrogation) or providing an answer (information).

But how do we guide our audience’s attention to the things they need to know?

                     the focal point
                      The focal point of an image is determined by:

                         Focus: Our eyes are drawn to a subject in sharp focus.

                           Contrast: Our eyes are drawn to the highest point of contrast.

                         Placement: Our eyes are drawn to a subject that has
                            prominent placement within the frame (or in relation to its
                              environment).


                      The focal point of moving images is determined by the
                           additional elements:

                           Faces: Our eyes are drawn to human faces, particularly one
                                that is expressing emotion.

                          Noise: Noise demands our attention, so our eyes are drawn to
                               the noisemaker within a frame.

                      Movement: Our eyes are drawn to a subject in motion.

How does having a focal point change now that we add the context of editing?
moving focal points
Because each image is preceded and followed by a new one, our focal point changes from
shot to shot. A focal point will change location within a shot when the camera moves or the
subject moves.

       reframing focal points
          Consider making the focal point of your composition a misdirection from a
          key piece of information in a frame. If you do this, you can create a sense of
           “discovery” when the audience’s eye finally goes from the primary point of
           interest to the secondary item.

guiding the eye
The placement of the focal point within the frame at the end of a shot will be a determining factor of
how visible or invisible a cut will be when transitioning to the next shot.
invisible cuts:
Making the cut between shots feel invisible can help the characters or subjects in each scene feel
more connected, and the audience remain immersed.
visible cuts:
Feeling the cut between shots can be helpful to show a disconnection or conflict between
characters or subjects.

The closer in proximity the focal point of one frame is to the next, the less distance the
viewer’s eye has to travel to follow the action.

close proximity between two
focal points after an edit:
less awareness of self, maintains
flow, building a more immersive
experience.


far proximity between two
focal points after an edit:
more awareness of self, creates
a more disjointed, interactive
experience.

grouping

The geographic organization of
characters within a scene establishes
their relationship to one another.
Characters standing in a group or on
the same side of the frame represent a
unified viewpoint of the scene.

Characters on opposing sides of the
frame or isolated from the group relay a
lack of unity or an opposing perspective.

how do I feel about it?
It’s not only what’s seen that matters, but how it’s interpreted. How an image will be
interpreted will depend on which perspective you see. Which perspective we see is essential
to how we think and feel about the situation! When creating a shot, we first need to choose if
we’re going to shoot it objectively or subjectively.

objective vs subjective shots
We need objective images to create logic.
We need subjective images to build emotion.





                objective                     subjective
      A shot where no particular character’s   A shot where we follow a character’s
             perspective is being expressed.                     perspective.


Let’s say a screenplay says:
Character A walks through a hallway and rounds the corner,
running into character B.

        Shooting subjectively might look like:
         a) We stay with A the entire time... and are startled with her.

        Shooting objectively might look like:
        b) We’re omniscient. We see A walking down the hallway and B coming down
        the other side.
        This could create suspense (“Oh no, what’s going to happen?!)
        or anticipation (“Oh no! They are going to run into each other! She’s going to
        embarrass herself!”)

subjective vs subjective shots
When shooting subjectively, whose perspective we’re seeing is important!

 Let’s say we’re filming a confrontation, two characters at odds with each other.

We could:
 a) See a big, towering man looking down at us.
 We’ll probably get nervous for the underdog. (“Oh no, he’s going to get slaughtered! I don’t want him
 to get hurt!”)

On the other hand, we could:
 b) See a small, nervous man looking up at us.
Maybe then we feel annoyed or confident! (“That little pipsqueak is so arrogant! He’s going to have to
 deal with the consequences of picking a fight!”)

So ask yourself:
- Does this shot need to convey information or feeling/logic or emotion/plot or theme?
- Which character do you want your audience to empathize with in this scene?
- Which character’s perspective will set up the next scene best?
- How do the compositions support that intention?

exercises


    1. scene analysis - practicing the 180 line

  Review the following sequence from the John Hughes film, “The Breakfast Club”.

  Use the overhead layout on the next page to draw a diagram of the
   following items (in order):

    1. Where you believe each camera setup was located for each still in the sequence.
    2. Where you believe the director established each new 180 line within the scene.
    3. Which direction each actor’s eye lines are facing throughout the scene.

2. shoot a scene on your phone

When blocking a scene with your actors, shoot video of your intended shots on your phone.
Send this material to your editor. They can try cutting the scene together and tell you if there
are any errors. This can save you the hassle of potential reshoots!

For complex sequences (e.g., action scenes, sex scenes, musical numbers) be sure to account
for blocking adjustments in your production schedule. Even better, if you hold rehearsals with
your cast, shoot it then and practice cutting it ahead of time!

3. recreate a scene
Select a scene from one of your favorite films (or use the scenes from The Breakfast
Club or Ocean’s Eleven), then use the following prompts to create a shotlist and/or
storyboards of how you would shoot this scene.

a) Is there anything you think could be improved? Can you identify any problems they may
have run into? Is there an opportunity to make it more interesting?

b) What does it look like in your signature style?

c) Would the scene have more moving shots? or more static shots? Would you move the
characters around throughout the space?

d) Would you shoot it more economically? Would you shoot more closeups? or fewer? Would
you add more specialty shots (profile, fisheye, dutch angle)?

e) Would you explore the space (still lifes of the decor, atmosphere of the space or the
geometry of the room)?

f) Would you focus on details about what’s being said (coverage of the blueprints in Ocean’s
Eleven, images that emphasize adjectives in the dialogue or an ECU of someone’s lips or ears)?
Would you focus on who the characters are (details about their styling or posture, reactions to
the information or a bouncing knee)?

h) Would you focus on a different character at a particular moment? What happens if you
make a different character the anchor or point of focus?
